# CDC Investigates Multistate Salmonella Outbreak

ATLANTA, Georgia (CNN) -- The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention is collaborating with public health officials across 42 states to identify the source of an outbreak involving a particular strain of salmonella known as Typhimurium. Salmonella bacteria are typically transmitted to humans through the consumption of contaminated food.

According to the CDC, at least 388 individuals have contracted this strain since September 3, though the majority of cases were reported between October 1 and December 31. Approximately 18 percent of those affected required hospitalization, with patients ranging in age from two months to 98 years.

California has reported the highest number of cases, with 55 confirmed infections, followed by Ohio (53), Massachusetts (39), Minnesota (30), and Michigan (20). The remaining 37 affected states have each reported between one and 19 cases. Notably, eight states—Montana, New Mexico, Louisiana, Mississippi, South Carolina, Florida, Alaska, and Hawaii—have not reported any cases linked to this outbreak.

State public health officials in Minnesota announced Friday that King Nut peanut butter has been identified as the source of an outbreak that may have contributed to one death in that state. CNN was unable to reach the company for comment. The CDC, however, has not yet determined the specific food or foods responsible for the broader national outbreak. CDC officials and state health workers are conducting case-control studies, tracing individuals infected as far back as September to identify their dietary exposures and pinpoint a common source.

**Learn more about salmonella »**

The Food and Drug Administration and the U.S. Department of Agriculture remain in close communication with the CDC; however, their involvement remains limited until the cause of the outbreak is definitively established.

Various strains of salmonella have historically been linked to outbreaks stemming from contaminated eggs, meat, poultry, vegetables, pet food, and even peanut butter. In one notable precedent, contaminated tomatoes were blamed for a salmonella Typhimurium outbreak in the fall of 2006, which sickened at least 183 people across 21 states. Most victims in that outbreak experienced diarrhea and fever lasting approximately one week, though no fatalities were reported.

Salmonella infections, caused by bacteria, can be treated with antibiotics when necessary, although certain strains have developed resistance to these medications, according to the CDC. Most infected individuals develop diarrhea, fever, and abdominal cramps within a few days of exposure, with symptoms typically lasting up to a week. While most patients recover without medical intervention, some may experience dehydration severe enough to require hospitalization. According to the National Institutes of Health, young children, elderly individuals, and those with compromised immune systems face the highest risk of severe complications.

Until the source of the outbreak is confirmed, the CDC recommends the following precautions:

- Thoroughly cook all meats, poultry, and eggs.
- Avoid consuming raw or unpasteurized milk and dairy products.
- Wash produce thoroughly before consumption.
- Prevent cross-contamination between uncooked meats and produce.
- Wash hands frequently during food preparation to minimize the risk of spreading salmonella.

# Salmonella Outbreak Investigation Spans Dozens of States

ATLANTA, Georgia (CNN) -- Health officials across 42 states are collaborating with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to pinpoint the origin of a Typhimurium salmonella outbreak. This bacterial illness typically spreads when people consume tainted food products.

CDC data reveals that a minimum of 388 individuals have contracted this particular strain since early September, with the bulk of infections clustering between October and the end of December. Roughly one in five affected patients required hospital care, and those sickened span an extraordinary age range—from infants just two months old to elderly patients approaching 99 years.

California leads all states in reported cases at 55, with Ohio close behind at 53. Massachusetts follows with 39 cases, while Minnesota and Michigan report 30 and 20 cases respectively. The remaining 37 affected states each show case counts ranging from single digits up to 19. Notably, eight states—Montana, New Mexico, Louisiana, Mississippi, South Carolina, Florida, Alaska, and Hawaii—have reported zero cases tied to this outbreak.

Minnesota health authorities announced Friday that they've traced their outbreak connection to King Nut brand peanut butter, potentially linking it to one fatality in their state. Attempts by CNN to reach the manufacturer for a statement proved unsuccessful.

Nationally, however, the CDC has yet to pinpoint the specific food source driving the broader outbreak. Investigators are conducting comparative case studies—essentially interviewing infected individuals dating back to September about their dietary habits—hoping to identify shared consumption patterns that might reveal the culprit.

Both the FDA and USDA remain in communication with CDC officials, though their role stays limited until the actual contamination source gets identified.

Salmonella outbreaks have historically stemmed from various contaminated products including eggs, meat, poultry, produce, pet food, and peanut butter. A notable precedent occurred in fall 2006, when tainted tomatoes triggered a Typhimurium outbreak affecting at least 183 people across 21 states—though that incident resulted in no deaths, with most victims experiencing roughly a week of fever and diarrhea.

This bacterial infection generally responds to antibiotic treatment, though the CDC notes growing resistance in certain strains. Typical symptoms—diarrhea, fever, and stomach cramping—emerge within days of exposure and can persist for about a week. While most patients recover without medical intervention, some develop dehydration severe enough to warrant hospitalization. The National Institutes of Health identifies very young children, elderly individuals, and those with weakened immune systems as facing the greatest risk for serious complications.

Pending confirmation of the outbreak's source, the CDC advises the public to:

- Cook all meat, poultry, and eggs thoroughly
- Steer clear of unpasteurized dairy products and raw milk
- Wash fresh produce carefully before consumption
- Keep raw meats separate from produce to prevent cross-contamination
- Wash hands frequently throughout food preparation

# Multi-State Salmonella Outbreak Investigation Update

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), working in close collaboration with public health officials across 42 states, has confirmed that it is actively investigating a significant multi-state outbreak of Salmonella Typhimurium. According to the latest figures, the outbreak has resulted in at least 388 reported infections since it was first identified in September. Health officials describe this as a widespread and concerning public health situation, given both the number of cases and the geographic spread across nearly the entire country.

Despite the scale of the outbreak, investigators have not yet been able to pinpoint the specific food product responsible for the widespread infections. To address this gap, epidemiologists and public health researchers have initiated case control studies, a standard epidemiological method used to compare the dietary habits and exposures of infected individuals against those of a similar but unaffected control group. These studies are designed to help identify patterns or common exposures that could reveal the source of the contamination, but as of now, no definitive food item has been confirmed as the cause.

In a related development, officials in Minnesota have identified a possible connection between the outbreak and King Nut peanut butter, a product that has been linked to at least one possible fatality in the state. # Atlanta: The Heart of the South

Atlanta, the capital of Georgia, stands as one of the most influential cities in the American South. Known for its rich history, vibrant culture, and significant role in the Civil Rights Movement, Atlanta has grown into a major economic and cultural hub over the decades.

The city holds particular significance in the media industry, as it serves as the headquarters for CNN (Cable News Network), one of the world's most recognizable news organizations. Founded by Ted Turner in 1980, CNN revolutionized broadcast journalism by becoming the first television channel to provide 24-hour news coverage. The CNN Center in downtown Atlanta remains an iconic landmark, drawing visitors interested in touring the studios and learning about the network's history.

Beyond its media presence, Atlanta is celebrated for its diverse economy, which includes sectors such as logistics, technology, film production, and finance. The city is home to Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport, one of the busiest airports in the world, reflecting Atlanta's role as a major transportation hub connecting the southeastern United States to the rest of the globe.

Atlanta's cultural landscape is equally impressive, featuring world-class museums, a thriving music scene, and numerous universities, including the historic Atlanta University Center, home to several historically Black colleges and universities. The city's connection to civil rights history is embodied in sites like the Martin Luther King Jr. National Historical Park, honoring the legacy of one of Atlanta's most famous native sons.

As Georgia's largest city, Atlanta continues to grow as a center of innovation, media, and Southern culture, balancing its historical roots with a forward-looking vision for the future.

# CDC Investigates Multi-State Salmonella Outbreak Linked to Unknown Source, Dozens Sickened

**(CNN)** — Federal health officials are investigating a growing outbreak of Salmonella Typhimurium that has sickened at least 87 people across 14 states, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

The outbreak, first identified through genetic sequencing that linked several cases to a common source, has prompted an active investigation by the CDC, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), and state health departments. Officials say the source of the contamination has not yet been confirmed, though early interviews with sickened individuals point to a possible link to fresh produce.

"We are working closely with our state and local partners to identify the source of this outbreak as quickly as possible," said a CDC spokesperson. "Whole genome sequencing shows these illnesses are closely related genetically, which suggests that people in this outbreak got sick from the same source."

## State-by-State Case Counts

According to the CDC's most recent data, illnesses have been reported in the following states:

- **Texas:** 14
- **California:** 12
- **Ohio:** 9
- **Florida:** 8
- **Illinois:** 7
- **Pennsylvania:** 6
- **New York:** 6
- **Georgia:** 5
- **North Carolina:** 5
- **Michigan:** 4
- **Arizona:** 4
- **Missouri:** 3
- **Tennessee:** 2
- **Colorado:** 2

Health officials note that the actual number of people sickened is likely much higher than reported, as many cases of salmonellosis go undiagnosed or unreported. The CDC estimates that for every confirmed case of salmonella, roughly 29 additional cases go unreported.

## Symptoms and Timeline

Illness onset dates range from early last month to just over a week ago, according to the CDC. Of the cases with available data, at least 19 people have been hospitalized, though no deaths have been reported at this time.

Symptoms of Salmonella infection typically include diarrhea, fever, and stomach cramps, appearing anywhere from six hours to six days after exposure. Most people recover without treatment after four to seven days, but in some cases — particularly among young children, older adults, and those with weakened immune systems — the infection can become severe enough to require hospitalization.

## Investigation Ongoing

Investigators are conducting interviews with sickened individuals to determine what they ate and where they shopped in the days before falling ill. The CDC says a specific food item has not yet been confirmed as the outbreak's source, and no recall has been issued at this time.

"We ask anyone with symptoms of salmonella infection to contact their healthcare provider," the CDC said in a statement. "And we will provide updates on specific food items to avoid as soon as more information is available."

The FDA is assisting with traceback efforts on any product samples collected from retail locations connected to reported illnesses.

## What Consumers Can Do

In the meantime, health officials are urging consumers to follow standard food safety practices, including:

- Washing hands thoroughly after handling raw food products
- Cooking meat and poultry to safe internal temperatures
- Refrigerating perishable foods promptly
- Washing fruits and vegetables under running water before consumption

This is a developing story. CNN will provide updates as new information becomes available from the CDC and FDA.

*—Reporting contributed by health and medical staff.*

# Salmonella Outbreak Linked to Peanut Butter Sickens Hundreds Nationwide

**National Health Alert**

Federal health officials have confirmed a widespread outbreak of *Salmonella Typhimurium* linked to contaminated peanut butter and peanut-containing products, prompting one of the largest food recalls in U.S. history.

## The Outbreak

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) reports that hundreds of illnesses across dozens of states have been traced back to peanut products manufactured by the Peanut Corporation of America (PCA) at its Blakely, Georgia facility. Health officials say the outbreak, which began in late 2008, has resulted in multiple deaths and hospitalizations, with vulnerable populations—including children, the elderly, and immunocompromised individuals—at greatest risk.

Salmonella infections typically cause diarrhea, fever, and abdominal cramps within 12 to 72 hours of exposure. While most healthy adults recover without treatment, severe cases can require hospitalization, and the infection can be life-threatening for high-risk groups.

## Investigation Findings

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), working alongside the CDC and state health departments, launched an investigation after clusters of illness were reported. Inspectors later discovered evidence suggesting the Georgia facility had unsanitary conditions and, troublingly, records indicating the company may have shipped products despite previous positive tests for salmonella contamination.

The investigation expanded rapidly as officials determined that PCA supplied peanut paste and peanut butter as ingredients to hundreds of other food manufacturers, affecting products ranging from crackers and cookies to ice cream and pet treats—not just jarred peanut butter sold directly to consumers.

## Recall Efforts

The FDA has been working with manufacturers to issue recalls affecting thousands of products. Consumers are urged to check the FDA's website and manufacturer recall lists before consuming any peanut butter or peanut-containing products purchased recently, particularly institutional or bulk-sized containers often used in schools and care facilities.

## Prevention Tips for Consumers

Health officials offer the following guidance:

- **Check recall lists regularly** via FDA.gov or CDC.gov for updated product information
- **Avoid products** made with bulk peanut butter or paste until cleared by health authorities
- **Practice food safety basics**: wash hands thoroughly before and after handling food
- **Watch for symptoms**: seek medical attention if experiencing severe diarrhea, high fever, or signs of dehydration
- **Don't taste-test** to determine if a product is safe—contamination cannot be detected by smell, taste, or appearance
- **When in doubt, throw it out**—do not attempt to salvage recalled products

## Ongoing Response

Officials continue to update the public as the investigation unfolds, with additional product recalls expected. The CDC emphasized that consumers should remain vigilant and consult official recall lists rather than relying solely on news reports, as new products are being added to affected lists regularly.

*This is a developing story. Consumers with questions about specific products should contact the manufacturer directly or consult FDA.gov for the most current recall information.*

---

*For the latest updates, contact your local health department or visit CDC.gov and FDA.gov.*

- Avoiding cross-contamination by using separate cutting boards for raw meats and produce
- Refrigerating perishable foods promptly

**Seek medical attention** if experiencing severe symptoms, including diarrhea lasting more than three days, high fever, blood in stool, or signs of dehydration such as reduced urination or dizziness.

Health officials are also urging clinicians to consider salmonellosis in patients presenting with compatible gastrointestinal symptoms and to report confirmed cases promptly to local health departments to aid the ongoing investigation.

## What Happens Next

The CDC has indicated it will provide updates as the investigation progresses, including any product recalls or expanded case counts. State health departments are continuing to interview affected individuals to identify common exposures, and laboratory testing is ongoing to confirm whether cases across different states share a genetic match, which would confirm a single contamination source.

Consumers are encouraged to monitor official channels—including the CDC website and FDA recall announcements—for the most current information as this developing situation unfolds.
